title: Protein Modules: SH2, SH3, PTB, PDZ and PH

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A {{c1::motif}} is a short amino-acid sequence, a few residues long, that a binding domain can recognise.
cards.quote: A motif is a short amino-acid sequence, a few residues long, that such a reader can recognise.

cards.front: Why can a cell switch a phosphotyrosine docking site on and off without making or destroying a protein?
cards.back: Kinases add the phosphate, which puts two negative charges on a small surface patch, and phosphatases can remove it within seconds.
cards.quote: The cell can therefore switch a docking site on and off without making or destroying a protein.
cards.section: Why a mark needs a reader

cards.front: A modular interaction domain {{c1::folds by itself}}, recognises a motif or lipid, and keeps that binding activity in another protein.
cards.quote: A modular interaction domain is a protein segment, from a few dozen to roughly two hundred amino acids, that folds by itself, recognises a motif or lipid, and keeps that binding activity in another protein.
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: A sarcoma-virus kinase with about a hundred residues altered just before its kinase domain phosphorylates tyrosine about as well as the original in a test tube. In rat cells its kinase activity is low and it no longer makes cells cancerous. What does the mismatch suggest about the altered region?
cards.back: The region has a job other than catalysis: holding other proteins and steering the kinase beside them. This region was named SH2.
cards.quote: That mismatch points to a job other than catalysis, holding other proteins and steering the kinase beside them, which a test-tube assay of phosphate transfer cannot see.
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: An SH3 domain is cut out of protein A and fused to an unrelated enzyme that cannot normally bind proline-rich peptides. The hybrid now binds the peptide that protein A's SH3 domain bound. What property of SH3 domains does this show?
cards.back: The domain folds on its own and carries its binding preference to a new protein. That is the definition of a modular domain.
cards.quote: A modular interaction domain is a protein segment, from a few dozen to roughly two hundred amino acids, that folds by itself, recognises a motif or lipid, and keeps that binding activity in another protein.
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: What does an SH2 domain bind?
cards.back: A phosphotyrosine and the residues just after it.
cards.quote: a phosphotyrosine and the residues just after it
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: What motif does an SH3 domain bind?
cards.back: A proline-rich motif with a PxxP core.
cards.quote: a proline-rich motif with a PxxP core
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: What does a PDZ domain read?
cards.back: The last few residues at a protein's C-terminal end, including its free carboxyl group.
cards.quote: the last few residues at a protein's C-terminal end, including its free carboxyl group
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: Some PH domains bind {{c1::phosphoinositides}}, the phosphorylated lipids of the membrane.
cards.quote: phosphoinositides, the phosphorylated lipids of the membrane, for some PH domains
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: A PDZ-binding tail gains one extra residue at its carboxyl end, and the old final residues are still present. Can a PDZ domain read them as the same terminal motif?
cards.back: No. The domain reads the last residues together with the free carboxyl end. The extra residue moves that end, so the old sequence is no longer the C-terminal target.
cards.quote: A PDZ domain reads the last residues together with the free carboxyl end.
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: Crk has no kinase activity, yet cells transformed by it carry more phosphotyrosine than normal cells. How?
cards.back: Crk reads phosphotyrosines through its SH2 domain and gathers the cell's own enzymes outside their usual arrangement.
cards.quote: it reads phosphotyrosines and gathers the cell's own enzymes outside their usual arrangement
cards.section: A module keeps its binding job when it moves

cards.front: Why can the phosphate grip alone not decide which SH2-containing protein binds a given phosphotyrosine?
cards.back: Many tyrosines are phosphorylated in a stimulated cell and around a hundred human proteins carry SH2 domains, so the phosphate does not single out a partner.
cards.quote: Many tyrosines are phosphorylated in a stimulated cell, and around a hundred human proteins carry SH2 domains, so the phosphate grip alone cannot choose a partner.
cards.section: SH2 specificity: two parts of one binding surface

cards.front: What are the two parts of an SH2 binding surface, and what does each hold?
cards.back: A pocket with lysine and arginine side chains holds the phosphotyrosine. A neighbouring groove holds the residues just after it.
cards.quote: lysine and arginine side chains in one pocket stacking against the phosphotyrosine ring and bonding to the phosphate, and a neighbouring groove holding the residues just after it
cards.section: SH2 specificity: two parts of one binding surface

cards.front: Purified SH2 domains are offered phosphopeptides with a fixed phosphotyrosine and random residues after it. Src-family domains select pTyr-Glu-Glu-Ile. Domains from p85, phospholipase C-gamma and SHPTP2 select pTyr-hydrophobic-any-hydrophobic. What does this show?
cards.back: Domains that all grip phosphotyrosine prefer different following residues, so the groove sets much of an SH2 domain's sequence preference.
cards.quote: Most other domains selected patterns of their own, so the groove sets much of an SH2 domain's sequence preference.
cards.section: SH2 specificity: two parts of one binding surface

cards.front: A Src-family SH2 domain has the arginine in its phosphate pocket mutated, but its groove is intact. Will it still pull pTyr-Glu-Glu-Ile peptides out of a phosphopeptide library?
cards.back: Not well. The groove only adds preference among phosphopeptides the pocket already holds; it cannot hold them alone.
cards.quote: The groove adds preference among phosphopeptides that the pocket already holds; it cannot hold them alone.
cards.section: SH2 specificity: two parts of one binding surface

cards.front: A phosphopeptide library has phosphotyrosine at position 0 and random residues at +1 to +3, each of the 20 amino acids equally likely. An SH2 domain pulls out peptides, and at +3 80 percent carry isoleucine, while +1 and +2 look like the library. By about how much is isoleucine enriched at +3, and what does it suggest?
cards.back: Isoleucine is 1 in 20, or 5 percent, of the library; 80 / 5 = 16-fold. A strong preference at one position suggests a separate pocket reading +3.
cards.quote: tested that with a peptide library: phosphotyrosine at a fixed position, random residues after it, sampled by purified SH2 domains
cards.section: SH2 specificity: two parts of one binding surface

cards.front: For one independent binding site at equilibrium, fraction of domain bound = {{c1::[ligand] / (Kd + [ligand])}}.
cards.quote: fraction of domain bound = [ligand] / (Kd + [ligand])
cards.section: How much is bound?

cards.front: An SH2 domain has Kd = 2 µM for a phosphopeptide, with one independent binding site at equilibrium. What fraction of domains is bound at 6 µM free peptide?
cards.back: Fraction = 6 / (2 + 6) = 0.75, so 75 percent. Kd is the free-ligand concentration at half occupancy.
cards.quote: Kd is the free-ligand concentration at which half the domains are occupied.
cards.section: How much is bound?

cards.front: Why does reversible SH2 binding matter for a phosphotyrosine site?
cards.back: While bound, the SH2 domain shields the phosphotyrosine. When it releases, a phosphatase can reach the site, and once the phosphate is gone that contact cannot re-form.
cards.quote: while an SH2 domain is bound it shields phosphotyrosine, but when it releases, a phosphatase can reach the site.
cards.section: How much is bound?

cards.front: How does c-Src hold itself in an inactive shape?
cards.back: Csk phosphorylates tyrosine 527 in the tail. The folded-back tail's phosphotyrosine sits in the SH2 pocket and the linker sits in SH3, pressing both domains against the back of the kinase.
cards.quote: Crystal structures confirm the clamp the second film draws.
cards.section: Src: a protein that reads itself

cards.front: In chicken c-Src, Csk phosphorylates {{c1::tyrosine 527}} in the tail.
cards.quote: Csk phosphorylates tyrosine 527 in the tail, six residues from the end in chicken Src.
cards.section: Src: a protein that reads itself

cards.front: Why can an outside phosphotyrosine ligand open the c-Src clamp?
cards.back: The internal tail fits the SH2 domain less well than a good ligand does, so the internal contacts are weak enough to be displaced.
cards.quote: An outside ligand wins because the tail after tyrosine 527 fits SH2 less well than phosphotyrosine–glutamate–glutamate–isoleucine
cards.section: Src: a protein that reads itself

cards.front: Why is viral v-Src always on?
cards.back: It has lost the tail and tyrosine 527 with it, along with some point mutations, so its clamp never forms.
cards.quote: v-Src's missing tail, as the second film showed, leaves it with no clamp.
cards.section: Src: a protein that reads itself

cards.front: Tyrosine 527 of c-Src is changed to phenylalanine, which cannot be phosphorylated. Predict kinase activity and whether cells are transformed.
cards.back: Activity rises and cells transform, like v-Src. With no phosphotyrosine in the tail, the SH2 domain has nothing to grip, so the clamp cannot form.
cards.quote: Changing tyrosine 527 to phenylalanine in c-Src has the same activating effect and makes it transform cells.
cards.section: Src: a protein that reads itself

cards.front: c-Src loses its amino-terminal myristate but keeps an intact phosphorylated tail. Which changes most directly: membrane anchoring or the SH2-tail grip?
cards.back: Membrane anchoring. The fatty acid is at the amino end, whereas the SH2-binding phosphotyrosine is in the carboxy-terminal tail.
cards.quote: The fatty acid is at the amino end, whereas the SH2-binding phosphotyrosine is in the carboxy-terminal tail.
cards.section: Src: a protein that reads itself

cards.front: Relative to wild-type c-Src at 1.0, kinase activity is 12 for Y527F and 9 for a mutant whose SH2 pocket cannot bind phosphotyrosine. The double mutant reads 11. What does this suggest?
cards.back: Both mutations break the same clamp, one at the tail phosphotyrosine and one at the pocket that grips it, so the double mutant gains nothing more. It rests on the rule that the phosphorylated tail held in SH2 is the brake.
cards.quote: Changing tyrosine 527 to phenylalanine in c-Src has the same activating effect and makes it transform cells.
cards.section: Src: a protein that reads itself

cards.front: How can a pathway gain a connection without new chemistry?
cards.back: Join a binding domain to an enzyme that already works, and a receptor can recruit that enzyme.
cards.quote: A pathway can gain a connection without new chemistry: join a reader to an enzyme that already works, and a receptor can recruit that enzyme.
cards.section: The virtue of modularity: new pathways from old parts

cards.front: In a proposed route, a proline-rich partner such as beta-arrestin binds the SH3 domain of c-Src, while the tail phosphotyrosine stays in SH2. What happens to the clamp?
cards.back: The clamp is thought to loosen, because SH3 is one of its two internal contacts. This is one of several routes that refine the clamp model without replacing it.
cards.quote: A proline-rich partner such as beta-arrestin can take the SH3 domain, a proposed route from an activated beta-adrenergic receptor to Src
cards.section: Several routes can open Src

cards.front: A designed protein joins a PIP3-binding PH domain to an SH2 domain for a receptor's phosphotyrosine motif. Each grip alone is too weak, together they hold. Cells get growth factor plus a PI 3-kinase inhibitor, and the receptor is still phosphorylated. Where is the protein?
cards.back: Mostly in the cytosol. Without PIP3 only one weak grip is available, and the protein stays at the membrane only where a receptor tail and PIP3 are both within reach.
cards.quote: Like the second film's coincidence detector, it stays only where a receptor tail and PIP3 are both within reach.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A PH domain fused to a fluorescent protein has a membrane-to-cytosol ratio of 1.0 before growth factor and 4.5 after. With a PI 3-kinase inhibitor the ratio after growth factor is 1.1, and with a basic pocket residue changed to alanine it is 1.0. What do these data support?
cards.back: The domain is recruited by a lipid that PI 3-kinase makes, whose head group binds the basic pocket. Recruitment needs PI 3-kinase activity and the pocket.
cards.quote: PIP3 is a lipid made on the inner face of the membrane when PI 3-kinase phosphorylates PIP2.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An Akt PH domain is used as the PIP3 reader in a detector. Which other lipid, made when PI 3-kinase is active, could also recruit it, and what should you do for a strict PIP3 detector?
cards.back: PI(3,4)P2 could also recruit it. For a strict PIP3 detector, choose a PH domain known to prefer PIP3.
cards.quote: The Akt PH domain would work, but it also binds PI(3,4)P2, so for a strict PIP3 detector choose a PH domain known to prefer PIP3.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a detector, PH, SH2 and a Ca2+-dependent C2 domain are each too weak alone, and all three are needed. A cell-permeant Ca2+ chelator is added after growth factor stimulates PIP3 and the receptor. Predict recruitment and why.
cards.back: Recruitment is abolished. C2 binds acidic membrane lipids only when it has Ca2+ bound, so without Ca2+ only two weak grips remain.
cards.quote: For calcium, add a Ca2+-dependent C2 domain, which binds acidic membrane lipids only when it has Ca2+ bound.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does an SH2 domain's motif preference not uniquely fix its partner in a cell?
cards.back: Motif preference narrows the candidates, but location, abundance, timing, scaffold-imposed proximity, competition among related domains and the cell's kinases and phosphatases also contribute.
cards.quote: Motif preference narrows the candidate set but does not uniquely specify an in-cell partner.
cards.section: More than the motif

cards.front: An SH2 domain has Kd = 0.5 µM for a phosphopeptide at one independent site. What free peptide concentration gives 90 percent of the domains bound?
cards.back: 0.9 = L / (0.5 + L) gives L = 9 × 0.5 = 4.5 µM. A lower Kd would need less ligand for the same occupancy.
cards.quote: A lower Kd means less ligand is needed for the same occupancy.
cards.section: How much is bound?

cards.front: In the PH–SH2 detector, a PI 3-kinase inhibitor, verified to remove PIP3, still leaves the protein at the membrane after stimulation. How do you interpret this and what do you change?
cards.back: The SH2 grip alone is too strong. The design needs a poorer SH2 or PH domain so that no single grip suffices.
cards.quote: If removing one input, verified as truly removed, still leaves the protein at the membrane, the other grips are too strong and the design needs a poorer SH2 or PH domain.
cards.section: Design problem
